title: Accelerator
idea: A drum machine that can only speed up, until it crashes and starts again.
how: Press PLAY. The tempo climbs on its own; ACCEL sets how hard you press the pedal and BRAKE (or B) drops it back. Click the squares to change the pistons (kick, snare, hat). At 240 BPM the machine crashes, rebuilds its pattern and pulls away again. Your samples become the pistons, pitched up as the speed rises.

manifesto.name: The Founding and Manifesto of Futurism
manifesto.author: Filippo Tommaso Marinetti
manifesto.where: Le Figaro, Paris, 20 February 1909
ideas: Speed, machines and danger are the new beauty; the past (museums, libraries, academies) should be swept away.
A roaring racing car is more beautiful than the Victory of Samothrace (paraphrase of point 4).
Art should be aggressive and full of energy, not contemplative.
quotes: Time and Space died yesterday.
manifesto.system: Tempo is the only thing that matters and it only ever increases. The past is never kept: every crash throws away the old pattern and builds a new one. The engine drone follows the speed, so velocity itself becomes the melody.

design.name: Plakatstil (German 'poster style')
design.who: Lucian Bernhard, Ludwig Hohlwein, Hans Rudi Erdt
hallmarks: One object, shown big and flat, on a plain ground
The brand name in heavy hand-drawn letters, and nothing else
Few flat colours, strong silhouettes, no decoration
works: Lucian Bernhard, Priester matches poster (1905)
Lucian Bernhard, Manoli cigarettes posters (about 1910)
Hans Rudi Erdt, Opel poster (1911)

title: Intonarumori
idea: Six noise machines, one for each of Russolo's six families of noise, cranked by hand.
how: Press PLAY. Each column is one family of noise. Drag up and down inside a column to crank its pitch, click its name to switch it on or off, and click the dots to change its rhythm. Your samples feed family 5 (percussion) and family 6 (voices).

manifesto.name: The Art of Noises (L'arte dei rumori)
manifesto.author: Luigi Russolo
manifesto.where: open letter to Francesco Balilla Pratella, Milan, 11 March 1913
ideas: Machines have filled modern life with noise, so music should use noise instead of only 'pure' musical sounds.
Noise can be tuned and controlled: Russolo built intonarumori (noise intoners) cranked by hand, with a lever for pitch.
He sorted noise into six families: roars and booms; whistles and hisses; whispers and murmurs; screeches and buzzes; percussion on metal, wood, skin and stone; and voices of animals and people.
quotes: We must break out of this narrow circle of pure sounds and conquer the infinite variety of noise-sounds.
manifesto.system: Each of the six families is its own noise machine with a crank (pitch) and a rhythm. There are no notes and no scales, only tuned noise, as in Russolo's intonarumori.

design.name: Neville Brody
design.who: Neville Brody, art director of The Face and Arena
hallmarks: Big condensed type, often rotated or set vertically
Hand-drawn geometric symbols used as section markers
Black ground, red accents and a lot of energy
works: The Face magazine covers and spreads (1981 to 1986)
FF Blur typeface (1992)
FUSE experimental type magazine (from 1991, with Jon Wozencroft)

title: Enharmonic
idea: A quarter-tone melody machine in free metre, where every bar chooses its own length.
how: Press PLAY. Each block in the chain is one bar and its width is its number of beats. ENHARMONIC moves from ordinary semitones to quarter tones and free microtones. FREEDOM lets bar lengths swing further from 4. MACHINE turns up the factory pulse underneath. Your sample is the choir chord at the start of each bar, retuned in quarter tones.

manifesto.name: Manifesto of Futurist Musicians
manifesto.author: Francesco Balilla Pratella
manifesto.where: Milan, 11 October 1910 (followed by the Technical Manifesto of Futurist Music, 1911)
ideas: Young composers should leave the conservatories and academies and study freely (paraphrase).
The Technical Manifesto called for the 'enharmonic' mode, using intervals smaller than a semitone.
It also called for free rhythm, breaking out of fixed, regular bars, and for music that carries the soul of crowds, factories, trains and aeroplanes (paraphrase).
manifesto.system: Pitches move on a 24-step quarter-tone scale, with free detuning on top. Every bar picks its own number of beats, so the metre is never fixed, and a mechanical pulse runs underneath as the 'factory'.

design.name: Fortunato Depero
design.who: Fortunato Depero, Futurist painter and designer
hallmarks: Chunky, blocky lettering built from geometric pieces
Mechanical puppet figures and toy-like machines
Strong red, black and cream, with flat bright accents
works: Depero Futurista, the 'bolted book' (1927)
Campari advertising and the Campari Soda bottle (1932)
Casa d'Arte Futurista Depero, Rovereto

title: Cut-up Hat
idea: Your loop is cut into words, shaken in a hat and played back in the order the pieces come out.
how: Press PLAY. The loop is cut into slices and each slice gets a newspaper word. SHAKE THE HAT draws a new order, which then repeats faithfully, as Tzara's recipe says. Click a word to take it out of the hat (it goes silent). CHAOS reshakes on every pass. Drop any loop to cut it up.

manifesto.name: Dada Manifesto 1918
manifesto.author: Tristan Tzara
manifesto.where: read in Zurich on 23 March 1918, published in Dada 3
ideas: Dada rejects logic, systems and good taste; it is a protest against a culture that produced the First World War.
Meaning is suspect, so chance and nonsense are allowed into art.
Tzara's 1920 recipe 'To make a Dadaist poem' says: cut a newspaper article into words, shake them in a bag, and copy them out in the order they come out (paraphrase).
quotes: DADA DOES NOT MEAN ANYTHING
I am against systems; the most acceptable system is on principle to have none.
manifesto.system: The sample is the newspaper article and each slice is a word. Shaking the hat gives a chance order, which is then copied out 'conscientiously' on every pass, unless you choose chaos.

design.name: David Carson
design.who: David Carson, art director of Ray Gun
hallmarks: Overlapping, cropped and clashing type, often hard to read on purpose
Mixed typefaces and sizes in one layout, set at odd angles
Grungy texture; the reader's feeling matters more than legibility
works: Ray Gun magazine (1992 to 1995)
Ray Gun's Bryan Ferry interview set in Zapf Dingbats
The End of Print, book with Lewis Blackwell (1995)

title: Automatic
idea: Draw without stopping to think: your hand becomes a melody and an exquisite corpse in three parts.
how: Press PLAY. Drag inside one of the three panels (head, body, legs) and keep moving: height sets the pitch, left to right scrubs through your sample, and speed sets the volume. Let go and the drawing loops for ever. Each panel is hidden while you draw the next, as in the exquisite corpse game; REVEAL shows the whole creature and DREAM AGAIN wipes it. Starts with a seed drawing so it plays at once.

manifesto.name: Manifesto of Surrealism
manifesto.author: André Breton
manifesto.where: Paris, October 1924
ideas: Surrealism should free the mind from reason, logic and moral control, and let the unconscious speak.
Automatic writing: write fast, without a subject, without stopping to read back.
Dreams are as real and important as waking life. The Surrealists' 'exquisite corpse' game builds one figure from parts drawn by different people, each hidden from the next.
quotes: Psychic automatism in its pure state
dictated by thought, in the absence of any control exercised by reason
manifesto.system: You never pick a note: the gesture itself makes the sound, and each drawing replays as a dream loop. The three hidden panels are layered into one exquisite corpse.

design.name: Tadanori Yokoo
design.who: Tadanori Yokoo, Japanese graphic artist
hallmarks: Rising-sun rays and Hokusai-style waves mixed with pop imagery
Clashing hot colours: pink, red, turquoise and gold
Collage of postcards, comics and photos, often surreal and autobiographical
works: Having Reached a Climax at the Age of 29, I Was Dead (1965 poster)
Posters for Shūji Terayama's Tenjō Sajiki theatre (late 1960s)
Koshimaki Osen poster (1966)

title: Neo-Plastic Grid
idea: A Mondrian composition you can hear: vertical lines are time, horizontal lines are pitch, colours are instruments.
how: Press PLAY. The playhead sweeps left to right. Each coloured rectangle sounds when the playhead reaches it and lasts as long as it is wide. Red plays your sample, blue is bass, yellow is a bell and black is a drum. Click a rectangle to change its colour (red, yellow, blue, black, white). COMPOSE draws a new grid; + LINE splits the time or pitch again.

manifesto.name: De Stijl Manifesto I
manifesto.author: Theo van Doesburg, Piet Mondrian, Vilmos Huszár, Antony Kok and others
manifesto.where: De Stijl magazine, Leiden, November 1918
ideas: Art should move from the individual to the universal, from the old consciousness of time to the new.
Neo-Plasticism (Mondrian): only straight horizontal and vertical lines, the three primary colours, and the non-colours black, white and grey.
Balance comes from unequal but equivalent parts, never from symmetry.
quotes: There is an old and a new consciousness of time.
manifesto.system: Only horizontal and vertical divisions exist. Vertical lines cut time, horizontal lines cut pitch, and the three primaries plus black are the only instruments. Rectangle sizes are durations, so the whole composition is one balanced, unequal grid.

design.name: Wim Crouwel
design.who: Wim Crouwel ('Mr Gridnik'), co-founder of Total Design
hallmarks: Everything sits on a visible, strict grid
Modular letters built from straight strokes and rounded corners
Calm sans type, lots of white, small coloured accents
works: New Alphabet typeface (1967)
Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam posters and catalogues (1964 to 1985)
Vormgevers poster (1968), with its grid printed on the poster

title: Building
idea: Build a song floor by floor from Bauhaus shapes: blue circles, red squares, yellow triangles.
how: Press PLAY. The music climbs the building from the ground floor up, one floor per bar, and each floor has four beats. Click a cell to place a shape: ● blue circle plays a bass and fifth, ■ red square plays a slice of your sample, ▲ yellow triangle plays quick metal hits. Higher floors are higher in pitch. Fill every floor and a roof chord completes the building.

manifesto.name: Programme of the Staatliches Bauhaus in Weimar
manifesto.author: Walter Gropius
manifesto.where: Weimar, April 1919, with Lyonel Feininger's woodcut 'Cathedral' on the cover
ideas: All the arts should join together in building; the old wall between artist and craftsman should go.
Students train in workshops, as apprentices, journeymen and masters.
Teachers at the Bauhaus (Kandinsky, Itten) taught basic forms and colours as a shared language.
quotes: The ultimate aim of all visual arts is the complete building!
Architects, sculptors, painters, we must all return to the crafts!
manifesto.system: The song is a building: floors are bars and cells are beats. The three basic Bauhaus shapes in Kandinsky's colours are the only crafts allowed, and the piece is only complete when every floor has been built.

design.name: Herbert Bayer
design.who: Herbert Bayer, Bauhaus student, then head of its print and advertising workshop
design.era: Dessau, 1925 to 1928, then Berlin and the USA
hallmarks: Lowercase only: Bayer argued capitals were unnecessary
Geometric sans letters built from circles and straight lines
Primary colours, bold bars and diagonal layouts
works: Universal alphabet (1925)
Poster for Kandinsky's 60th birthday exhibition (1926)
Design for a newspaper kiosk (1924)

title: Kinetic Rhythms
idea: Three rotating rods sweep through points in space; every crossing is a note, so rhythm comes from motion, not mass.
how: Press PLAY. Three rods turn at different speeds. Click anywhere in the circle to add a point and shift-click (or right-click) to remove one. When a rod passes over a point it sounds, with distance from the centre setting pitch. The red rod plays your sample, the black rod a tone and the grey rod a click. Change the speed ratios with the sliders to get polyrhythms.

manifesto.name: The Realistic Manifesto
manifesto.author: Naum Gabo and Antoine Pevsner
manifesto.where: printed as a poster for their open-air exhibition, Tverskoy Boulevard, Moscow, 5 August 1920
ideas: Art must be built on space and time, the real elements of life, not on imitation.
Volume is not mass: depth and space are the material of sculpture, so open constructions replace solid lumps.
Kinetic rhythms, motion itself, become a basic element of art (Gabo's 'Kinetic Construction', 1919 to 1920, was a vibrating steel rod).
quotes: Space and time are the only forms on which life is built and hence art must be constructed.
manifesto.system: Nothing here is a fixed note on a grid. Sound appears only where moving rods meet points in space, so the rhythm is the kinetic rhythm of the construction and you shape it by changing space and speed.

design.name: Gustav Klutsis
design.who: Gustav Klutsis, Latvian-Soviet Constructivist designer
hallmarks: Dynamic diagonals and photomontage
Red, black and white with bold condensed lettering
Designs for agitprop radio-orator stands and kiosks with loudspeakers
works: Electrification of the Entire Country (1920 photomontage)
Designs for Radio-Orator stands (1922)
Spartakiada posters and postcards (1928)

title: Zero of Form
idea: Pure shapes float on white; each one is a held tone, and where they overlap your sample sparkles.
how: Press PLAY. Every shape is a sustained sound: height is pitch, size is loudness, and the kind of shape sets the timbre (square: pure tone, bar: reedy, circle: your sample looped, cross: noise). Drag shapes to move them and double-click empty white to add a new one. Shapes drift slowly by themselves; where two overlap, grains of your sample spark. The black square is the bass drone.

manifesto.name: From Cubism and Futurism to Suprematism: The New Painterly Realism
manifesto.author: Kazimir Malevich
manifesto.where: Petrograd, published for the 0.10 exhibition, December 1915, where the Black Square was first shown
ideas: Painting should stop copying objects and nature; pure geometric forms on a white ground are enough.
Malevich called this the 'zero of form': start again from nothing, from the Black Square.
Later he described Suprematism as the supremacy of pure feeling in art (The Non-Objective World, 1927).
manifesto.system: There are no melodies and no beats, only non-objective forms. Each shape's position, size and type become a pure sustained sound, and the white field is silence. The music is made from feeling, by placing forms.

design.name: El Lissitzky
design.who: El Lissitzky, painter, designer and typographer
hallmarks: Suprematist shapes turned into communication: wedges, circles and bars
Diagonal tension, red and black on white
Typography as architecture, the book as a constructed object
works: Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge (1919 poster)
Of Two Squares: A Suprematist Tale in Six Constructions (1922)
For the Voice, Mayakovsky's poems designed by Lissitzky (1923)

title: Zaum
idea: Type words that mean nothing in any language and a throat made of your sample sings them.
how: Press PLAY. The words in the megaphone are sung syllable by syllable: vowels are sung through vocal formant filters, and consonants become hisses, clicks, trills and hums. Type your own transrational words, or press INVENT for new ones (or ask Gemini, if you have a key). Your sample becomes the singer's throat. Pitch follows the letters.

manifesto.name: A Slap in the Face of Public Taste
manifesto.author: David Burliuk, Aleksei Kruchenykh, Vladimir Mayakovsky and Velimir Khlebnikov
manifesto.where: Moscow, December 1912
ideas: The past is too tight: the classics should be thrown off the ship of modernity.
Poets have the right to enlarge their vocabulary with arbitrary and newly made words (paraphrase).
This led to zaum, 'beyond-sense' language. Kruchenykh's poem 'Dyr bul shchyl' (1913) is written in words that belong to no language.
quotes: Throw Pushkin, Dostoevsky, Tolstoy, etc., etc. overboard from the Ship of Modernity.
manifesto.system: Words are judged only by their sound. Each letter has a sound rule: vowels are sung shapes of the mouth and consonants are noises. Meaning never comes into it, so the machine sings any invented language.

design.name: Alexander Rodchenko
design.who: Alexander Rodchenko, Constructivist designer and photographer, often with Mayakovsky
hallmarks: Bold sans letters set along diagonals and blocks
Black, red and cream, with a woman shouting through a megaphone of type
Photomontage and steep camera angles
works: Books (Lengiz poster with Lilya Brik, 1924)
Pro Eto, Mayakovsky's book with Rodchenko's photomontages (1923)
Advertisements for Mosselprom and Dobrolet, with Mayakovsky's texts (1923 to 1925)

title: Theory of Intervals
idea: A film strip of sample 'shots', where the loudest music happens in the cuts between them.
how: Press PLAY. Each frame on the strip is a shot: a piece of your sample with its own speed and length. Between shots is an interval, and it sounds as a sweep from one shot to the next, bigger when the shots are more different. Drag a frame up or down to change its speed, click a gap to change its kind of cut, and press MONTAGE to re-edit the order. EYE spins the poster spiral faster.

manifesto.name: WE: Variant of a Manifesto
manifesto.author: Dziga Vertov (the Kinoks group)
manifesto.where: Kino-Fot magazine, Moscow, 1922
ideas: Cinema should give up borrowed drama and literature and record life as it is, through the machine eye.
Montage is the organisation of the visible world, and movement is its material.
The intervals, the passages from one movement to the next, are what make up the art (paraphrasing Vertov).
quotes: Intervals (the transitions from one movement to another) are the material, the elements of the art of movement.
manifesto.system: Shots are just short pieces of the sample. The machine puts its weight on the intervals: every cut generates its own sound from the difference between the shot before and the shot after, so editing the order changes the music.

design.name: Vladimir and Georgii Stenberg
design.who: Vladimir and Georgii Stenberg, Soviet film poster designers
hallmarks: Dizzying perspective, spirals and figures falling through space
Projected and enlarged film stills drawn by hand with a projection device
Saturated magenta, orange and black, with tall condensed letters
works: Man with a Movie Camera (1929 poster for Vertov's film)
Battleship Potemkin (1929 poster)
The General (1929 poster for Buster Keaton's film)

title: BLAST / BLESS
idea: Every instrument is a word on the wall: BLAST it and it hits hard and dirty, BLESS it and it turns soft and holy.
how: Press PLAY. Click a word to cycle it: off, then BLAST (loud, distorted, short), then BLESS (gentle, sustained, reverberant). Your sample is the word SAMPLE. Drag the vortex in the corner: round and round raises the energy, and the centre of the vortex is stillness, where everything drops to half time.

manifesto.name: BLAST, Manifesto of the Vorticists
manifesto.author: Wyndham Lewis, with Ezra Pound, Gaudier-Brzeska and others
manifesto.where: BLAST No. 1, London, published June/July 1914 in a puce-pink cover
ideas: Lists of things to BLAST and things to BLESS, set in huge black type.
The Vortex: a point of maximum energy, and at its centre a point of stillness.
Against both sentimental Victorian England and Italian Futurism, while sharing its love of the machine.
quotes: BLAST HUMOUR
BLESS the HAIRDRESSER
manifesto.system: The only controls are BLAST and BLESS. Every sound has a blasted and a blessed version, and the vortex sets the energy, with stillness at its centre.

design.name: Paula Scher
design.who: Paula Scher, Pentagram partner
hallmarks: Type as image: huge mixed wood-type letters fill the whole surface
Words stacked, tilted and cut off at the edges, like a loud street wall
Few colours, maximum volume
works: Bring in 'da Noise, Bring in 'da Funk posters for The Public Theater (1995)
The Public Theater identity (1994)
Painted maps series (from the 1990s)

title: Event Scores
idea: A deck of Fluxus-style instruction cards; the machine performs whichever card is on top, then flips the next.
how: Press PLAY. The top card is performed for about eight seconds, then the next card is drawn. Each card is a tiny instruction (drip, repeat, count, stretch, swarm, hold, reverse, silence) carried out on your sample. Click a card in the deck to perform it now, press SHUFFLE to reorder, or ask Gemini (with a key) to write new cards. The cards here are written in the spirit of Fluxus event scores; they are not historical scores.

manifesto.name: Fluxus Manifesto
manifesto.author: George Maciunas
manifesto.where: a collaged leaflet handed out at the Festum Fluxorum Fluxus, Düsseldorf, February 1963
ideas: Purge the world of 'Europanism', dead art and professional, commercial culture.
Art should be living, playful and understandable by everyone, a flood of non-art reality.
Fluxus artists (George Brecht, Yoko Ono, Alison Knowles, La Monte Young) wrote short event scores: a few words to be performed by anyone.
quotes: Purge the world of bourgeois sickness
PROMOTE A REVOLUTIONARY FLOOD AND TIDE IN ART
manifesto.system: The music is not composed: it is a deck of plain instructions that anyone, including the machine, can perform. Each card is a small event, and the order is left to chance.

design.name: Experimental Jetset
design.who: Experimental Jetset (Marieke Stolk, Danny van den Dungen, Erwin Brinkers)
hallmarks: Helvetica-style grotesque, set big and simple, often lowercase
Flat primary-colour blocks and stripes, a language taken from modernism and punk
Systems over images: identities built from a few rules
works: Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam identity (2004)
Whitney Museum 'responsive W' identity (2013)
John & Paul & Ringo & George T-shirt (2001)

title: Dérive
idea: A walker drifts through a psychogeographic city; each district has its own sound, and the city's pull decides the route.
how: Press PLAY. The walker drifts through the city map, pulled by the districts and by chance. Your footsteps are tiny grains of your sample. Each district is a different treatment of your sample (market, river, station, arcade, wasteland, bridge), and you hear it more strongly the closer the walker gets. Drag the walker to take it somewhere, or drop arrows (click the map) to change the currents. DÉTOURNEMENT hijacks the current district: reversed, re-pitched and cut up.

manifesto.name: Report on the Construction of Situations
manifesto.author: Guy Debord
manifesto.where: written for the founding of the Situationist International at Cosio di Arroscia, Italy, July 1957
ideas: Constructed situations: moments of life deliberately built from a unity of setting and events.
Psychogeography: the study of how city spaces act on feelings and behaviour, with the dérive (drift) as its method.
Détournement: hijacking existing images and words and turning them against their first meaning.
manifesto.system: The tool does not loop through a song. It sets up a city of sound districts and a walker who drifts through them. The music is the record of that drift, so the city's contours build the situation, and détournement lets you hijack whatever district you are in.

design.name: Jamie Reid
design.who: Jamie Reid, artist and designer for the Sex Pistols, influenced by the Situationists
hallmarks: Ransom-note lettering cut from newspapers
Fluorescent pink, yellow and green with black halftone
Détourned images, such as the Queen with a safety pin
works: God Save the Queen sleeve (1977)
Never Mind the Bollocks sleeve (1977)
Suburban Press (1970 to 1975)

title: Painted Lines
idea: Paint melodies by hand in screen-print layers; the loop prints one colour at a time, then all of them together.
how: Press PLAY. Pick an ink, then paint on the sheet: left to right is time and height is pitch. Each ink is a voice and plays a continuous gliding line wherever you painted: pink is your sample, sung; yellow is a pure lead; blue is the bass; green is a brushed noise. The sheet prints layer by layer, one ink per pass, and then all inks together. WASH SCREEN clears the current ink.

manifesto.name: The Stuckists manifesto
manifesto.author: Billy Childish and Charles Thomson
manifesto.where: London, August 1999
ideas: A call for painting as the central art, made by hand, against conceptual art and ironic gesture.
The artist should be emotionally involved and willing to be seen to fail, not hide behind cleverness.
They called themselves Stuckists after Tracey Emin told Childish his art was 'stuck'.
quotes: Artists who don't paint aren't artists.
manifesto.system: There are no presets, patterns or randomness: the only way to make sound is to paint it with your hand. The wobble of your stroke is the wobble of the melody, and nothing gets quantised.

design.name: Corita Kent
design.who: Sister Corita Kent, artist, teacher and screen-printer at Immaculate Heart College
hallmarks: Overprinted translucent screen-print inks, bright and joyful
Hand-written texts and lyrics cut into and over advertising type
Big words, torn shapes and the energy of protest and pop
works: tomato (1964 serigraph)
power up (1965)
Rainbow Swash, Boston gas tank (1971)

title: Vow of Chastity
idea: One sample, no effects, no grid: you play it live by hand, and every rule you break goes in a public confession.
how: Press PLAY. A take loops for four bars. Press the keys A S D F G H J K (or click the pads) to play your sample from eight cue points, live, with handheld timing wobble. What you play is recorded into the take. The rules are switched on. Untick a rule to break it (for example to allow reverb or quantising), and the break is written into the confession. CLEAR TAKE starts again.

manifesto.name: Dogme 95 Manifesto and Vow of Chastity
manifesto.author: Lars von Trier and Thomas Vinterberg
manifesto.where: Copenhagen, read out in Paris in March 1995
ideas: Ten rules for film-making: shoot on location; sound must never be produced apart from the images; the camera must be handheld; no optical work or filters; no superficial action; no genre films; the director must not be credited.
A 'rescue action' against the cosmetics of technology and cinema as illusion.
Directors who broke a rule wrote confessions.
manifesto.system: The vow is the instrument. There is one location (your sample), no added sound and no effects; timing is handheld, so nothing is quantised, and nothing is a genre preset. Breaking a rule is allowed, but it is confessed in writing.

design.name: Brutalist web design
design.who: Brutalist websites, a movement named and catalogued by Pascal Deville (brutalistwebsites.com, 2014)
design.era: the web, 1990s plain HTML, revived 2014 onwards
hallmarks: Default browser styles: Times, blue underlined links, grey buttons
Raw structure on show, with no decoration and no polish
Honest, hard-edged, sometimes deliberately ugly
works: brutalistwebsites.com (Pascal Deville, 2014)
Drudge Report (plain HTML since the 1990s)
Craigslist (craigslist.org, 1995 to now)

title: Credo
idea: Three coins tossed six times build an I Ching hexagram, and the hexagram picks the sound, its length and its loudness from a chart.
how: Press PLAY. For each event the machine tosses three coins six times to build a hexagram (1 to 64), which picks one of 64 sounds from the chart (slices of your sample, tones, noises and silences). Two more hexagrams pick its duration and its dynamics. Changing lines (old yin or old yang) turn the sound into a second sound part way through. You can lock a row of the chart to exclude it, or press LISTEN to let the noise of the room in.

manifesto.name: The Future of Music: Credo
manifesto.author: John Cage
manifesto.where: given as a talk to the Seattle Arts Society, 1937; printed in Silence (1961)
ideas: Noise is music: composers should use the whole field of sound, including the sounds of electrical instruments.
Rhythmic structure should replace harmony as the basis of composition.
Later (Music of Changes, 1951) Cage used I Ching coin tosses and charts so that his likes and dislikes did not decide the music.
quotes: Wherever we are, what we hear is mostly noise. When we ignore it, it disturbs us. When we listen to it, we find it fascinating.
manifesto.system: Every decision is made by chance: coin tosses build hexagrams, and the hexagrams read a chart of 64 sounds, 64 durations and 64 dynamics. Your only jobs are to set up the chart (your sample) and to listen.

design.name: Ikko Tanaka
design.who: Ikko Tanaka, Japanese graphic designer
hallmarks: Flat planes of pure colour forming simple geometric figures
Japanese tradition (Noh, Rimpa, kabuki) reduced to modernist geometry
Large space, a grid and calm, confident shapes
works: Nihon Buyo poster (1981), the geometric geisha face
Muji art direction, co-founder (from 1980)
Sharaku poster series (1990s)

title: Breath Squares
idea: Four nested squares are four drones that breathe; colours that sit close together make their tones beat against each other.
how: Press PLAY and listen. The squares breathe on their own, slowly. Hold the mouse button (or touch) anywhere to breathe in and let go to breathe out; the drones follow your breath, each a little later than the one inside it. Click a square to change its colour. Each colour has its own pitch, and two neighbouring colours that are close in hue make slow beats, so you can hear the interaction of colour. The outer square is your sample, stretched into air.

manifesto.name: Sonic Meditations
manifesto.author: Pauline Oliveros
manifesto.where: written with the ♀ Ensemble at the University of California, San Diego, 1971; Oliveros later named the wider practice Deep Listening (1989)
ideas: Short text pieces for anyone, often with no musical training, built from breathing, listening and making long tones.
Oliveros distinguished focused attention from global, open awareness, and asked listeners to move between the two.
Listening is the music: the aim is healing and noticing, not performance.
manifesto.system: There is no rhythm or melody to compose. The tool slows sound down to breath. The four drones follow your breathing in and out, and your job is to listen to how they change, especially the slow beating where two tones meet.

design.name: Josef Albers
design.who: Josef Albers, Bauhaus teacher, then at Black Mountain College and Yale
hallmarks: Three or four squares nested, set low on the canvas
Flat colour relationships: the same colour looks different next to different neighbours
Plain, calm type, with colour doing all the work
works: Homage to the Square series (1950 to 1976, over 1,000 works)
Interaction of Color (1963 book)
Two Structural Constellations, Corning Glass Building, New York (1959)

title: BECAUSE
idea: A three-chord punk machine where your BECAUSE lines become the riffs and the shouted rhythm.
how: Press PLAY. Write your own BECAUSE lines. Each line is one section of the song: the number of letters in each word picks the chord (only three chords, I, IV and V, are allowed), and the syllables are shouted in rhythm using your sample as the voice. Press SCREAM for a chorus. Press + LINE to add a section. DIY: the more lines you add, the longer the song.

manifesto.name: Riot Grrrl Manifesto
manifesto.author: Kathleen Hanna (with Bikini Kill)
manifesto.where: Bikini Kill zine no. 2, Olympia, Washington, 1991
ideas: A list of lines that each start with BECAUSE, giving the reasons girls need to make their own culture.
Do it yourself: make your own records, zines and shows rather than waiting for the industry.
Support and encourage each other instead of competing, and refuse the idea that girls cannot play.
manifesto.system: The song is written entirely in BECAUSE lines that you write yourself. The machine turns every word into a chord from a three-chord DIY set and every syllable into a shout. No skill is needed: if you can write a line, you can make a song.

design.name: Barbara Kruger
design.who: Barbara Kruger, American conceptual artist and former magazine designer
hallmarks: Black-and-white found photographs
Futura Bold Oblique, white on red bars
Direct address with words like I, you, we and your
works: Untitled (Your body is a battleground), 1989
Untitled (I shop therefore I am), 1987
Untitled (Your gaze hits the side of my face), 1981

title: Cyborg
idea: Three boundary sliders (human/animal, organism/machine, physical/non-physical) blur one groove between flesh and code.
how: Press PLAY. A groove plays, built from your sample. Drag the three sliders to break three boundaries. HUMAN to ANIMAL turns the voice into calls and chirps. ORGANISM to MACHINE moves from loose, breathy timing to locked, square, bit-crushed code. PHYSICAL to NON-PHYSICAL dissolves the sound into grains and space. Click the pixel face to scramble its genes, which re-rolls the pattern.

manifesto.name: A Cyborg Manifesto
manifesto.author: Donna Haraway
manifesto.where: Socialist Review, 1985, as 'A Manifesto for Cyborgs'; revised in Simians, Cyborgs, and Women (1991)
ideas: The cyborg, a hybrid of machine and organism, is a figure for refusing fixed identities and dualisms.
Haraway names three boundary breakdowns: human and animal, organism and machine, physical and non-physical.
Pleasure in the confusion of boundaries, and responsibility in building them.
quotes: I would rather be a cyborg than a goddess.
manifesto.system: The three boundaries Haraway lists become the three controls. Nothing is purely human or purely machine: every sound sits at a point between them, and you move it by blurring the borders.

design.name: April Greiman
design.who: April Greiman, Los Angeles designer, an early adopter of the Apple Macintosh
hallmarks: Bitmap pixels, low-resolution video stills and digital artefacts
Layered space, gradients and floating planes
New Wave typography mixing technology and the body
works: Does It Make Sense? (Design Quarterly 133, 1986), a life-size digital self-portrait poster
Pacific Wave exhibition poster (1987)
Identity for China Club, Los Angeles (1980)

title: Virus Matrix
idea: A step grid that is also a living culture: a virus spreads through the pattern each cycle, corrupting the notes it touches.
how: Press PLAY. Each column is a step and each row is a slice of your sample. Pink cells are healthy notes; green cells are the virus, which plays a mutated, crushed and reversed version of the sound. After every cycle the culture grows: the virus spreads to neighbouring notes and dies after three cycles, and new notes grow back in the gaps. Click to plant notes (click again for the virus, again to clear). INFECT seeds the virus; PATCH heals everything.

manifesto.name: A Cyberfeminist Manifesto for the 21st Century
manifesto.author: VNS Matrix (Josephine Starrs, Julianne Pierce, Francesca da Rimini, Virginia Barratt)
manifesto.where: Adelaide, first shown as a billboard and later in the game-art piece All New Gen (1993)
ideas: Women hijacking technology from inside, written as a gleeful, bodily, rude text.
The virus as a figure: something inside the system that rewrites it.
Against 'big daddy mainframe': play, saboteurs and slime instead of control.
quotes: we are the virus of the new world disorder
manifesto.system: The pattern is not fixed. A virus lives in it and rewrites it from within, cycle after cycle, so the groove corrupts itself and grows back. You can plant and patch, but you can't stop the culture.

design.name: Y2K web aesthetic
design.who: The late-1990s and early-2000s look of the web, music videos and electronics
hallmarks: Chrome, liquid metal and glossy jelly buttons
Iridescent gradients, lens flares and pixel stars
Wide techno fonts and translucent plastics like the iMac G3
works: Apple iMac G3 in Bondi Blue (1998)
The Designers Republic and Wipeout game graphics (1995 to 1999)
Hype Williams music videos, such as Missy Elliott's The Rain (1997)

title: Change Nature
idea: The harmonic 'laws' of music are editable: choose the octave, the number of notes in it and how the overtones stretch.
how: Press PLAY. A chord machine plays a progression. Nothing about the tuning is fixed: EDO sets how many equal steps divide the octave (12 is normal; try 5, 7, 19, 22 or 31). OCTAVE stretches the octave itself away from 2:1. OVERTONES stretches the harmonics of every tone so that the timbre matches the new tuning. Your sample is tuned into the same system. NATURALISE resets to 12, 2:1 and harmonic; ALIENATE picks a strange world.

manifesto.name: Xenofeminism: A Politics for Alienation
manifesto.author: Laboria Cuboniks (Helen Hester, Diann Bauer, Amy Ireland, Katrin Kolo, Lucca Fraser, Patricia Reed)
manifesto.where: published online, 2015; later in Helen Hester's book Xenofeminism (2018)
ideas: Nothing should be accepted as fixed or given just because it is called natural.
Alienation is a starting point for freedom: technology can be repurposed for emancipation.
An anti-naturalist, gender-abolitionist and rationalist feminism.
quotes: If nature is unjust, change nature!
manifesto.system: In most music tools, the octave, twelve notes and the harmonic series are treated as nature. Here they are controls. You change the 'natural' laws of tuning and timbre, and the machine rebuilds its harmony in the world you have made.

design.name: M/M (Paris)
design.who: M/M (Paris): Michaël Amzalag and Mathias Augustyniak
hallmarks: Hand-drawn alphabets laid over photographs
Fashion, music and art mixed in one playful, layered language
Bright pastel collage, with letters drawn as if by a child or a scientist
works: Björk, Vespertine and Medúlla artwork (2001, 2004)
Yohji Yamamoto catalogues with Inez & Vinoodh (1990s)
The Alphabet, with Inez & Vinoodh (2001)

title: Auto-Destructive Loop
idea: A loop that destroys itself as it plays; its slow death is the piece, shown as a wall of bananas turning from green to brown.
how: Press PLAY. Your sample loops in 48 pieces, one banana per piece. Every pass, acid eats into the loop: pieces fade, crackle, drop out and at last fall silent, and their bananas ripen and rot. LIFETIME sets how many passes the work survives (from a few moments to many minutes). When it has all gone, the work is finished; press REBUILD to make a new one. Click a banana to rot that piece straight away.

manifesto.name: Auto-Destructive Art (manifestos 1 to 3)
manifesto.author: Gustav Metzger
manifesto.where: London: the first manifesto is dated 4 November 1959; Metzger gave a public demonstration on the South Bank in 1961, painting acid onto nylon
ideas: Art whose own process of disintegration is the work.
A public art for industrial societies, a response to the bomb and mass destruction.
Each work has a lifetime, and when the disintegration is complete the work is over.
quotes: Auto-destructive art is primarily a form of public art for industrial societies.
manifesto.system: The loop is built to decay: each pass damages it further, permanently, until it falls silent. You choose its lifetime, but you cannot save it. The destruction is the music.

design.name: Stefan Sagmeister
design.who: Stefan Sagmeister, Austrian designer in New York (Sagmeister & Walsh)
hallmarks: Type made from real, often perishable things: bananas, the body, coins, food
Handwriting and craft rather than slick finish
Personal maxims from his list 'Things I have learned in my life so far'
works: Banana wall, 'Self-confidence produces fine results', Deitch Projects (2008): 10,000 bananas that changed colour as they ripened
AIGA Detroit poster with type cut into his own skin (1999)
Lou Reed, Set the Twilight Reeling sleeve (1996)

title: Art Concret
idea: Every voice is a written formula, step × a + b mod n, so the whole piece is constructed in the mind before a sound is made.
how: Press PLAY. Each of the six rows is a voice defined by four whole numbers. A step sounds when (step × a + b) mod n is less than k. The arcs show each voice as a Müller-Brockmann concert circle. Change the numbers with the arrows or by scrolling over them. There is no randomness at all: the same numbers always make the same music. Row 3 plays your sample at the position the formula points to.

manifesto.name: The Basis of Concrete Painting (Art Concret)
manifesto.author: Theo van Doesburg, Otto G. Carlsund, Jean Hélion, Léon Tutundjian and Marcel Wantz
manifesto.where: the single issue of the magazine Art Concret, Paris, April 1930
ideas: A painting should be built entirely from purely plastic elements, planes and colours, which mean nothing but themselves.
The work should be fully constructed in the mind before it is made.
The technique should be mechanical, exact and impersonal, not lyrical or by hand.
manifesto.system: Each sound is a concrete fact made from integers, with no expression, randomness or reference. You construct the piece as arithmetic, and it plays back exactly the same every time.

design.name: Josef Müller-Brockmann
design.who: Josef Müller-Brockmann, Swiss designer and author of Grid Systems in Graphic Design (1981)
hallmarks: Strict mathematical grids, with sans-serif type flush left and ragged right
Abstract geometry (circles, arcs, bands) as visual music
Objective, unsentimental communication
works: Tonhalle-Gesellschaft Zürich 'musica viva' concert posters (1950s to 1970s)
Der Film poster (1960)
Weniger Lärm (Less Noise) poster (1960)

title: Spatial Cuts
idea: A painted drone is the canvas; slash it, and each cut opens a window through which your sample comes from the space behind.
how: Press PLAY to hear the canvas, a flat coloured drone. Drag across the canvas to slash it. Each cut opens a window into space: its length sets how long the loop through it is, its angle sets the pitch, and its height sets where in your sample it looks. The more cuts, the more space and echo come through the surface. Click a cut to close it, and change the canvas colour with the swatches (each colour is a different drone).

manifesto.name: Manifiesto Blanco (White Manifesto)
manifesto.author: Lucio Fontana, with students at the Academia Altamira
manifesto.where: Buenos Aires, 1946; signed by students including Bernardo Arias and Horacio Cazeneuve
ideas: Art needs a new synthesis of colour, sound, movement, time and space, in step with science.
Leave the canvas and the static image behind for matter in motion.
This led to Spatialism (from 1947) and Fontana's cuts in the canvas (Concetto spaziale, Attese, from 1958).
manifesto.system: The surface (the drone) is not the work. The work is what you let through it. Each cut makes sound, space and time come from beyond the surface, so matter, colour and sound move together, as the manifesto asked.

design.name: Giovanni Pintori for Olivetti
design.who: Giovanni Pintori, art director of Olivetti's advertising office
hallmarks: Playful abstract shapes, numbers and dots standing for machines and calculation
Flat, bright colours on white or black, with lots of air
Small, elegant type set beside a big image
works: Olivetti Lettera 22 poster (1953)
Olivetti Elettrosumma 22 poster, the cascade of numbers (1956)
Olivetti logotype (1947)

title: Matter Alive
idea: Your sample is the ground: throw balls of mud, paint and paper onto its waveform, and every impact plays the sound at that spot.
how: Press PLAY. The landscape is the waveform of your sample. Click or drag anywhere to throw material onto it (choose MUD, PAINT or PAPER). Each ball falls, bounces on the waveform and plays the sample at the place where it lands, louder for harder hits. Mud is heavy and low and sticks quickly, paint splashes, and paper is light, high and bounces for a long time. Balls leave marks on the ground. SHAKE throws everything back into the air. When everything has settled, the machine throws a little more by itself.

manifesto.name: Gutai Art Manifesto
manifesto.author: Jirō Yoshihara
manifesto.where: Geijutsu Shinchō magazine, Tokyo, December 1956, for the Gutai Art Association (founded in Ashiya, 1954)
ideas: Do not distort materials into illusions: let the material speak and meet the human spirit directly.
Action, body and chance in direct contact with matter, as in Kazuo Shiraga's Challenging Mud (1955) and Saburō Murakami's paper-breaking pieces (1955 to 1956).
Do what has never been done before.
quotes: Gutai art does not alter the material. Gutai art imparts life to the material.
manifesto.system: The sample is not edited, filtered or sequenced. It stays as it is, as raw matter, and you bring it to life by throwing other matter at it. Every sound comes from a physical impact.

design.name: Yusaku Kamekura
design.who: Yusaku Kamekura, Japanese graphic designer, nicknamed 'the Boss'
hallmarks: A single bold red circle (the sun) above gold rings
Photographs of bodies in motion against black
Big sans type and strong, simple symbols
works: Tokyo 1964 Olympic posters, including the sprinters' start (1962)
Nikon posters (1950s)
Hiroshima Appeals poster (1983)

title: Bicho
idea: A hinged metal creature: bend its plates and the angles between them become the intervals of its chord.
how: Press PLAY. The creature is five plates joined by hinges. Drag any plate to fold it around its hinge. Each hinge angle sets an interval, so the shape of the creature is its chord, which is played as a slow arpeggio with your sample as the voice. Left alone, the creature moves very slowly by itself. Press a preset shape to snap into a new pose. As Lygia Clark said, the bicho has no back or front and answers your touch.

manifesto.name: Neo-Concrete Manifesto
manifesto.author: Ferreira Gullar, with Amilcar de Castro, Lygia Clark, Lygia Pape, Franz Weissmann, Reynaldo Jardim and Theon Spanúdis
manifesto.where: Jornal do Brasil, Rio de Janeiro, March 1959
ideas: A break with the rationalism and mechanism of São Paulo concrete art.
The work of art is not a machine but a quasi-corpus, closer to a living organism than an object.
Expression, sensation and the participation of the viewer, as in Lygia Clark's hinged metal Bichos (from 1960).
manifesto.system: The chord is not chosen from a list. It comes from the physical pose of a hinged creature that you handle, so harmony becomes something you touch and fold, and the creature answers by moving.

design.name: Alexandre Wollner
design.who: Alexandre Wollner, Brazilian designer who trained at the Ulm School of Design (HfG Ulm)
design.era: São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro, 1950s to 1970s
hallmarks: Concrete-art rigour applied to corporate identity
Geometric marks built on a grid, with flat colour and simple sans type
Brazil's first design office, Forminform (1958), and co-founder of the ESDI school in Rio (1963)
works: Poster for the 1st International Film Festival of Brazil, with Geraldo de Barros (1954)
Sardinhas Coqueiro logo and packaging (1958)
Banco Itaú visual identity (1970)

title: Anthropophagy
idea: Feed the mouth sounds from anywhere; it chews them into pieces and digests them into a new Brazilian rhythm.
how: Press PLAY. The mouth eats sounds: every sample you load is eaten, and so are the built-in sounds (click FEED to give it another). It chews each sound into pieces that go into the stomach. The rhythm (a baião, with zabumba, triangle and agogô parts) is played only with the digested pieces, and DIGEST rearranges which piece goes where, mixing everything it has eaten. Change the rhythm with the buttons. Nothing is played raw: everything foreign is devoured and made new.

manifesto.name: Manifesto Antropófago (Cannibal Manifesto)
manifesto.author: Oswald de Andrade
manifesto.where: the first issue of Revista de Antropofagia, São Paulo, May 1928, illustrated with Tarsila do Amaral's painting Abaporu
ideas: Brazilian culture should 'devour' European and other foreign culture, digest it and make something of its own.
A pun on Hamlet that sets Brazil's Indigenous Tupi in place of 'to be'.
Cannibalism as a cultural strategy, revived by Tropicália in the 1960s.
quotes: Tupi or not tupi, that is the question.
manifesto.system: No sound is ever played as it arrived. Everything you feed in is chewed into pieces and digested, and only those pieces make the rhythm. Foreign material becomes local music by being eaten.

design.name: Rogério Duarte
design.who: Rogério Duarte, Brazilian designer, poet and musician, a key graphic voice of Tropicália
design.era: Rio de Janeiro and Bahia, 1960s to 1970s
hallmarks: Psychedelic, Op-Art bands of colour radiating like a sun
Modernist clarity mixed with tropical exuberance and popular street lettering
Green, yellow and red, sometimes 'stained' as a political sign
works: Poster for Glauber Rocha's Deus e o Diabo na Terra do Sol (1964)
Cover for Gilberto Gil's 1968 album (with photographer David Drew Zingg)
Cover for Caetano Veloso's 1968 album

title: Ultra Metaphor
idea: Fuse two sound images into one metaphor: the rhythm of one drives the body of the other, with every ornament stripped away.
how: Press PLAY. Pick a first image (its rhythm and gesture) and a second image (its body and colour). The machine fuses them into one metaphor, so 'the train is a bird' plays bird chirps in the rhythm of a train. Your sample is the image called VOICE. STRIP removes ornament: turn it up to delete passing notes and decoration until only the essential element is left. SWAP turns the metaphor around.

manifesto.name: Ultraísmo
manifesto.author: Jorge Luis Borges
manifesto.where: Nosotros magazine, Buenos Aires, December 1921; Ultraism began in Spain in 1918 and Borges brought it to Argentina
ideas: Reduce lyric poetry to its primordial element: the metaphor.
Cut out connecting phrases and useless adjectives, and abolish ornament, confessional tone and obscurity.
Fuse two or more images into one, to widen its power of suggestion.
manifesto.system: Each sound is an image. The machine never layers sounds side by side: it fuses two into one metaphor, rhythm from the first and body from the second. The STRIP control is the second rule, cutting everything that is only ornament.

design.name: Jan Tschichold
design.who: Jan Tschichold, German typographer (later in Switzerland and Britain)
hallmarks: The New Typography: asymmetric layouts, sans-serif type and no ornament
Bars, rules and white space doing the structural work
Red and black only; later a return to classical book design at Penguin
works: Die neue Typographie (1928)
Phoebus-Palast cinema posters, Munich (1926 to 1927)
Penguin Composition Rules (1947)

title: Strident Radio
idea: Tune a wireless dial across a 1920s city: every station is a different broadcast of your sample, with static and howl in between.
how: Press PLAY. Drag the dial, or use the arrow keys, to tune between seven stations. Each station broadcasts your sample in a different way (a jazz band, a factory, the news in Morse, a tango orchestra, a choir and a strident siren). Between stations there is static and heterodyne whistle, so tuning itself is part of the music. AUTO lets the dial wander by itself. The closer you are to a station, the clearer it gets.

manifesto.name: Actual No. 1 (Comprimido estridentista)
manifesto.author: Manuel Maples Arce
manifesto.where: printed as a poster and pasted on walls in Mexico City, December 1921
ideas: Art should celebrate the modern city, machines, electricity, cars and radio.
Rejection of the academy and of nostalgic and religious art.
The Estridentistas loved the radio; Kyn Taniya (Luis Quintanilla) wrote 'Radio: poema inalámbrico en trece mensajes' (1924).
quotes: ¡Chopin a la silla eléctrica!
manifesto.system: The instrument is a radio. All the music is in the airwaves, and you tune through the noisy city to find it. The static and squeal between stations are as much a part of the piece as the stations.

design.name: Lance Wyman
design.who: Lance Wyman, American designer of wayfinding and identity systems
design.era: Mexico City, 1966 to 1970, then New York
hallmarks: Mexico 68 lettering: thick letters echoed by concentric parallel lines, influenced by Op Art and Huichol art
Bright, hot colours: magenta, orange, turquoise and green
Pictograms for metro stations and events, readable without words
works: Mexico 68 Olympics identity (1966 to 1968)
Mexico City Metro station pictograms (1969)
Minnesota Zoo identity (1980s)

title: Zenith
idea: An endless climb to the zenith: Shepard tones and a sample that rises forever but never arrives.
how: Press PLAY. Every voice climbs, and as each one gets too high it fades out while a new one fades in at the bottom, so the climb never ends (a Shepard–Risset glissando). Your sample rises with the tones, re-pitched in ever-higher layers. SPEED sets how fast you climb; BARBARIAN adds the drum of the barbarogenius, a heavy pounding Balkan rhythm in 7/8. Click the stage to fire a rocket of sample fragments towards the zenith.

manifesto.name: Manifesto of Zenitism
manifesto.author: Ljubomir Micić
manifesto.where: Zenit magazine, Zagreb, 1921 (later Belgrade), with Ivan Goll and Boško Tokin
ideas: The Barbarogenius: a 'barbarian' genius from the Balkans who will bring new life to a tired Western Europe.
Art aimed at the zenith, the highest point, as a cosmic and spiritual ascent.
An international avant-garde that links Expressionism, Futurism, Dada and Constructivism, from the edge of Europe.
manifesto.system: The music always climbs towards the zenith and never lands. The barbarian drum below, in an uneven Balkan metre, is the energy that drives the ascent.

design.name: Karel Teige
design.who: Karel Teige, Czech artist, typographer and theorist of the Devětsil group
hallmarks: Typographic picture-poems built from sans letters, photos, rules and diagonals
Poetism: modern life as play, with ports, aeroplanes, radio and the circus
Bold red-and-black Constructivist book covers
works: Abeceda (Alphabet), with Vítězslav Nezval and the dancer Milča Mayerová (1926)
Covers for the magazine ReD (1927 to 1931)
Cover for Jaroslav Seifert's Na vlnách TSF (1925)

title: Make It Bloom
idea: Don't sing the rose, make it bloom: build a new sound from nothing, partial by partial, then let it flower through your sample.
how: Press PLAY. Draw on the sixteen bars to build a new sound from its harmonics (partials). Each column is one partial, from the fundamental on the left upward. The created sound plays as a slowly changing chord. Your sample is not copied either: it is made to bloom through a bank of resonators tuned to your partials, so it takes on the colour of your creation. NON SERVIAM randomises everything you have made. FLOWER makes the partials open and close like petals.

manifesto.name: Non serviam and Creacionismo
manifesto.author: Vicente Huidobro
manifesto.where: Non serviam, a lecture in Santiago de Chile (1914); the poem Arte poética in El espejo de agua (Buenos Aires, 1916)
ideas: The poet should not imitate nature but create new things, just as nature creates trees.
Non serviam: the artist refuses to be nature's servant.
The poet as 'a little god'.
quotes: Por qué cantáis la rosa, ¡oh Poetas! / Hacedla florecer en el poema (Why do you sing the rose, oh Poets? Make it bloom in the poem)
manifesto.system: You do not record or imitate a sound: you build one from pure harmonics, and even your sample is only allowed to sound through the new thing you have made.

design.name: Alvin Lustig
design.who: Alvin Lustig, American graphic designer, typographer and teacher
design.era: Los Angeles and New York, 1940s to 1955
hallmarks: Abstract, symbolic book covers that capture a book's spirit rather than illustrate it
Modernist forms drawn from Klee, Miró and Constructivism
Hand-drawn marks combined with sans type and flat, earthy colour
works: New Directions book covers, including the New Classics series (from the 1940s)
The Ghost in the Underblows, Ward Ritchie Press (1940)
Covers for Noonday Press and Meridian Books (1950s)

title: Slow Cooker
idea: Time-stretch your sample until it slows to near stillness, simmering it in grains that you season and leave to ripen.
how: Press PLAY. Your sample is put in the pot and played back extremely slowly as a cloud of grains (up to 200 times slower) without changing its pitch. SLOWNESS sets how slowly the cooking head moves through the sound. SEASON adds tiny accents of salt (high grains) and herbs (lower octaves). Leave it alone: the longer it plays, the more the flavours ripen (the cloud gets denser and warmer). Clicking the bowl adds a single bell and nothing else.

manifesto.name: Slow Food Manifesto
manifesto.author: Folco Portinari, for the movement founded by Carlo Petrini
manifesto.where: signed in Paris in December 1989 at the founding of the international Slow Food movement
ideas: A defence against 'Fast Life', which disrupts our habits and our homes.
Material pleasure and slow, long-lasting enjoyment as the remedy.
Rediscover the flavours of local cooking and take time for them.
quotes: We are enslaved by speed.
manifesto.system: Nothing is hurried here. The sample, the 'ingredient', is cooked at extreme slowness, and the result improves the longer you leave it, with careful seasoning instead of more ingredients.

design.name: Kenya Hara
design.who: Kenya Hara, Japanese designer and art director of MUJI
hallmarks: Emptiness (utsuwa, the vessel) and the colour white as a space for meaning
Very quiet type and lots of space, with natural materials
Design as sensation, touch and 'haptic' experience
works: Art direction for MUJI (from 2002)
The book White (2008)
Opening and closing ceremony programmes for the Nagano Winter Olympics (1998)

title: Repurpose Platform
idea: Steer a vector between four futures and repurpose the machine itself: every corner is a whole groove, and you can always expand the map.
how: Press PLAY. Drag the cursor around the square. Each corner is a complete groove (FOLK LOOP, FACTORY, NETWORK and POST-WORK) and the music is a weighted blend of all four, recalculated every step. The arrow shows your vector. EXPAND throws all four corners into new, more extreme futures. Your sample is the raw material of every groove, cut up differently in each.

manifesto.name: #Accelerate: Manifesto for an Accelerationist Politics
manifesto.author: Alex Williams and Nick Srnicek
manifesto.where: published online in May 2013, later in the anthology #Accelerate (2014)
ideas: Rather than reject technology and go back to small local 'folk politics', repurpose existing technical platforms for collective ends.
Distinguishes mere speed from acceleration as navigation: experimenting and steering rather than just going faster.
Recover the ambition to build futures, rather than defend the present.
manifesto.system: There is no 'faster' button. You navigate: the music is a vector you steer between possible futures, and EXPAND keeps widening the space of options rather than returning to the old loop.

design.name: The Designers Republic
design.who: The Designers Republic, design studio founded by Ian Anderson in Sheffield, 1986
hallmarks: Corporate and consumer signs repurposed as satire, with fake logos and slogans
Dense, hyper-modern layouts in Japanese-inspired fluorescent colours
Electronic music sleeves and video game interfaces
works: Graphics for the video game Wipeout (1995)
Sleeves for Pop Will Eat Itself (late 1980s)
Sleeves for Warp Records artists (1990s)

title: Airport Loops
idea: Seven loops of different, unrelated lengths drift in and out of phase, so the music never repeats in the same way.
how: Press PLAY. Each ring is a tape loop with its own length in seconds (for example 17.8, 20.1, 31.8). Each loop carries a single note or your sample (loaded sounds enter on their loops straight away), and because the lengths share no common measure, the combinations never repeat exactly. Click a ring to mute or unmute it. DRIFT nudges all the lengths to new values. The music is designed to be ignored as much as listened to: leave it on in the background.

manifesto.name: Ambient Music (liner notes to Ambient 1: Music for Airports)
manifesto.author: Brian Eno
manifesto.where: sleeve notes for Ambient 1: Music for Airports, released on Polydor in 1978
ideas: Music as a tint or atmosphere for a place, in contrast to canned background music.
It should reward attention but never demand it.
Eno built parts of the album from tape loops of different lengths that drift out of sync.
quotes: Ambient Music must be able to accommodate many levels of listening attention without enforcing one in particular; it must be as ignorable as it is interesting.
manifesto.system: No sequencer, no bar line. Loops of unrelated lengths overlap, and the combinations never repeat in exactly the same way. Nothing ever demands your attention.

design.name: Peter Saville
design.who: Peter Saville, English graphic designer and co-founder of Factory Records
hallmarks: Minimal sleeves that often leave off the band name and title
Borrowed images from science, art history and industry, coded colour
Refined classical and modern type, used with restraint
works: Joy Division, Unknown Pleasures (1979), using a pulsar data plot
New Order, Power, Corruption & Lies (1983), with Fantin-Latour's roses and a colour-code alphabet
New Order, Blue Monday sleeve, shaped like a floppy disk (1983)

title: Idea Machine
idea: Write wall-drawing instructions and the machine executes them blindly: each line drawn across the grid becomes a melody.
how: Press PLAY. The list on the right is a set of instructions in the style of a wall drawing ('5 straight lines from the left edge to the right edge, in blue'). The machine carries them out on a 16 × 12 grid. Time runs from left to right and pitch from bottom to top, and every grid cell that a line passes through plays a note in that line's colour (one colour, one instrument). Change any field of an instruction, add (+) or delete (×) instructions, or press NEW for a random one. With a Gemini key, describe a feeling and Gemini writes instructions. The execution is the same every time: once the idea is fixed, the machine makes the art.

manifesto.name: Paragraphs on Conceptual Art
manifesto.author: Sol LeWitt
manifesto.where: Artforum, June 1967 (followed by Sentences on Conceptual Art, 1969)
ideas: The idea or concept is the most important part of the work; planning and decisions are made in advance.
Execution is a perfunctory affair, often done by others following written instructions, as in LeWitt's wall drawings (from 1968).
The aim is not to be emotional or clever but to make the work mentally interesting.
quotes: The idea becomes a machine that makes the art.
manifesto.system: You only write instructions. The machine executes them, without judgement, on a grid, and every line becomes notes. The same idea always gives the same music, while different machines (or different samples) give different 'executions'.

design.name: Otl Aicher
design.who: Otl Aicher, German designer and co-founder of the Ulm School of Design (HfG Ulm)
hallmarks: Strict grids and systems, with pictograms built from 45° and 90° angles
A non-political rainbow palette (light blue, green, orange and silver, with no red or black) for Munich 1972
Univers type, white space and modular identity rules
works: Munich 1972 Olympic identity and pictograms
Lufthansa corporate identity (from 1962)
The Rotis typeface family (1988)

title: No
idea: A full, flashy groove that you take apart with thirteen NOs, until only an ordinary walking pulse is left.
how: Press PLAY. The groove starts with everything: echo and reverb, fast fills, filter sweeps, a star lead, heroic chords, swing and moving pans. Each line on the right is one NO from the manifesto. Click it to say NO, and the matching element is removed from the music. Click again to take it back. Say NO to everything and you are left with a plain pulse built from your sample, like an ordinary task. NO TO INVOLVEMENT also locks your other controls.

manifesto.name: No Manifesto
manifesto.author: Yvonne Rainer
manifesto.where: published in the Tulane Drama Review (1965), after her dance Parts of Some Sextets; Rainer was a founder of Judson Dance Theater
ideas: A list of refusals: no to spectacle, virtuosity, magic, glamour, heroism and seduction.
Dance made from ordinary 'task-like' movement rather than display, as in Trio A (1966).
No to involvement of performer or spectator, and no to moving or being moved.
quotes: No to spectacle. No to virtuosity.
manifesto.system: Composition by subtraction. Each NO removes one kind of display from the music. The final state, with every NO on, is a plain pulse built from your sample: music as an ordinary task.

design.name: Massimo Vignelli
design.who: Massimo Vignelli, Italian designer who worked in New York with Lella Vignelli
hallmarks: A strict grid with very few typefaces, chiefly Helvetica
Coloured circles and bars on black or white, with a diagrammatic clarity
Ruthless reduction and consistency ('if you can design one thing, you can design everything')
works: New York City Subway map (1972)
American Airlines logo (1967)
The Vignelli Canon (2010)

title: Maintenance
idea: The music gets dirty and falls apart on its own; your job is to look after it, and the care itself becomes the rhythm.
how: Press PLAY. Four tracks play (DRUMS, BASS, CHORDS and your SAMPLE). Left alone they gather dust: notes drop out, the pitch sags, hiss builds up and the timing wanders. Use the four maintenance tasks on each track: SWEEP (removes dust and plays a brush rhythm), WASH (clears hiss with a rinse), TUNE (brings the pitch back with a tuning-fork tone) and OIL (puts the timing back with a squeak). Each task is a sound in its own right. The log counts your maintenance hours. Nothing is ever finished: maintenance never ends.

manifesto.name: Manifesto for Maintenance Art 1969! Proposal for an exhibition 'CARE'
manifesto.author: Mierle Laderman Ukeles
manifesto.where: typed proposal, New York, 1969; later she became unsalaried artist-in-residence at the New York City Department of Sanitation (from 1977)
ideas: Two systems: Development (the new, the avant-garde) and Maintenance (keeping it going, the daily work, mostly by women and workers).
Maintenance is a drag, takes all the time, and it is art too.
She proposed living in the gallery and doing her maintenance work as the exhibition.
quotes: after the revolution, who's going to pick up the garbage on Monday morning?
manifesto.system: There is no 'compose' mode here. The music decays by itself, and the only thing you can do is care for it. The care routines are the instruments, and your maintenance time is logged as the work.

design.name: Jock Kinneir and Margaret Calvert
design.who: Jock Kinneir and Margaret Calvert, British designers of public information
hallmarks: The UK road-sign system: white or yellow mixed-case type on blue, green or white panels with rounded corners
The Transport and Motorway typefaces
Simple pictograms (such as the 'men at work' and school children signs)
works: UK motorway and all-purpose road signs (from 1958, adopted through the Worboys Committee, 1963 to 1965)
The Transport typeface
Rail Alphabet for British Rail (1965)

title: Mould
idea: A rigid, straight step grid is slowly overgrown by mould, and wherever the mould spreads, the notes bend, drift and grow organic.
how: Press PLAY. The sequencer starts as a strict rectilinear grid of notes, perfectly straight and in time. Mould grows over it by itself, cell by cell. A mouldy note slides in pitch, drifts in time, swells and sprouts tiny spores (grains of your sample). Click to plant mould spores yourself, or press INVITE MOULD. RULER is the rationalist's tool: it scrapes everything clean and straight again, which the manifesto would not approve of. Turn the cells on and off by clicking with the right button (or Shift-click).

manifesto.name: Mould Manifesto against Rationalism in Architecture (Verschimmelungsmanifest)
manifesto.author: Friedensreich Hundertwasser
manifesto.where: read at Seckau Abbey, Austria, in July 1958
ideas: The straight line and rationalist, functional architecture are inhuman; he called the straight line godless.
Mould and decay are welcome: let moss and mould grow on the rigid surfaces of buildings, to bring them back to life.
People should be free to change their own walls and windows ('the right to the window').
manifesto.system: The grid is rationalism. The mould is life: it grows on its own, bending straight, quantised notes into glides, drifts and swells, while the RULER button shows how dull the clean version is.

design.name: Alphonse Mucha
design.who: Alphonse Mucha, Czech artist of Art Nouveau
hallmarks: Flowing, organic 'whiplash' lines, hair and vines
Women framed by circular halos and decorative mosaic panels
Soft pastel and gold palettes, with ornamental lettering
works: Gismonda poster for Sarah Bernhardt (1894 to 1895)
Job cigarette papers poster (1896)
The Seasons decorative panels (1896)

title: Ornament & Crime
idea: Decorate a plain melody with trills, turns and grace notes, but every ornament costs labour, and the bill and the fashion clock are always running.
how: Press PLAY. A plain melody (your sample sings the main notes) loops over eight steps. Click a note to cycle its ornament: none, grace note, mordent, turn and trill. The ORNAMENT slider adds ornaments everywhere at once. Each ornament adds to the LABOUR bill (Loos argued that ornament is wasted work, time and material), and ornamented notes go out of fashion: the more decorated a note is and the longer it plays, the more its sound fades and dulls. STRIP removes all ornament and resets the fashion clock.

manifesto.name: Ornament and Crime (Ornament und Verbrechen)
manifesto.author: Adolf Loos
manifesto.where: a lecture first given in Vienna (1910); printed in French in Les Cahiers d'aujourd'hui (1913)
ideas: Modern people should no longer need ornament; decorating everyday objects is a sign of the past.
Ornament wastes labour, money and material, and makes objects go out of style quickly.
Plain, well-made objects last, while ornamented ones become unfashionable.
quotes: The evolution of culture is synonymous with the removal of ornament from objects of everyday use.
manifesto.system: Ornament is allowed, but it is charged: every decoration costs labour on the bill and goes out of fashion over time, so its sound dulls, while plain notes stay fresh.

design.name: Koloman Moser
design.who: Koloman Moser, Austrian designer, painter and co-founder of the Wiener Werkstätte
hallmarks: Vienna Secession geometry: chequerboards, squares and repeating modules
Black and white contrasted with gold and a single accent colour
Stylised figures and lettering for posters, books and objects
works: Designs for the magazine Ver Sacrum (from 1898)
Stained-glass windows for the Kirche am Steinhof, Vienna (1904)
Austrian postage stamps for the 1908 Jubilee

title: The Store
idea: A corner shop of found sounds: every product on the shelves is a sound object, and whatever you put in your basket becomes the song.
how: Press PLAY. The shelves are stocked with sound products (cut from your sample and from built-in sounds), each with a price tag and a kind (THUMP, CLICK, HUM, VOICE, FIZZ or JINGLE). Click a product to add it to your basket. The basket is a loop: everything in it plays in the order you bought it. Click an item in the basket to return it. RESTOCK fills the shelves with new products. With a Gemini key, write 'I am for an art...' and Gemini stocks the shop with products that suit your line.

manifesto.name: I am for an art...
manifesto.author: Claes Oldenburg
manifesto.where: written for the catalogue of the show Environments, Situations, Spaces, Martha Jackson Gallery, New York (1961); the same year he opened The Store on East 2nd Street
ideas: A long list of 'I am for an art...' lines that celebrate everyday, commercial and street life.
Art made from cheap, found and popular things, like the painted plaster food and objects he sold in The Store (1961).
Against art that is precious and shut away.
quotes: I am for an art that is political-erotical-mystical, that does something other than sit on its ass in a museum.
manifesto.system: Sound comes from ordinary goods on a shelf. You compose by shopping: the basket is the sequence, and your line of 'I am for an art...' can restock the store.

design.name: Memphis Group
design.who: The Memphis Group, Milan collective founded by Ettore Sottsass in 1980 to 1981, with Michele De Lucchi, Nathalie Du Pasquier, George Sowden, Peter Shire and others
hallmarks: Clashing pastels and primaries, black-and-white squiggles and terrazzo-like patterns
Plastic laminate, bold geometric forms and deliberately 'bad taste'
Furniture and objects as playful, pop totems
works: Carlton room divider by Ettore Sottsass (1981)
Nathalie Du Pasquier's laminate and textile patterns (1981 onwards)
Peter Shire's Bel Air armchair (1982)

title: Scratch Orchestra
idea: A crowd of amateur players, each with their own scratch music, performing a sequence of rites chosen from the orchestra's constitution.
how: Press PLAY. Each circle is a player with their own little ostinato (their 'scratch music'), instrument and favourite note. Players come and go: ADD PLAYER recruits one more, click a player to send them home. Every eight bars the orchestra switches to a new RITE: TUTTI (everybody plays their scratch music), SOLO (one player only, the others accompany very softly), FOLLOW (everyone copies the leader, one by one), POPULAR CLASSIC (a familiar melody heard in fragments through your sample) or SILENCE AND BREATH. Choose the next rite yourself with the buttons.

manifesto.name: A Scratch Orchestra: draft constitution
manifesto.author: Cornelius Cardew
manifesto.where: The Musical Times, June 1969, London (founded with Michael Parsons and Howard Skempton)
ideas: An open orchestra of enthusiasts, trained or untrained, who pool their resources.
Each member keeps a notebook of 'scratch music', short accompaniments that can be played indefinitely.
Repertoire categories include Scratch Music, Popular Classics, Improvisation Rites, Compositions and a Research Project.
quotes: A Scratch Orchestra is a large number of enthusiasts pooling their resources (not primarily material resources) and assembling for action (music-making, performance, edification).
manifesto.system: The piece is a crowd, not a score. Each simulated player has their own scratch music, and the orchestra moves through the constitution's categories as rites, so the same players make very different music.

design.name: Ken Garland
design.who: Ken Garland, British graphic designer, writer and author of the First Things First manifesto (1964)
hallmarks: Bright, friendly primary colours and playful geometry
Clear, informative design for good causes and for play
Bold, simple sans-serif type
works: The First Things First manifesto (1964)
Catalogues, logo and toys for Galt Toys (1960s)
CND poster for the Aldermaston march, Easter 1962

title: Für Statik
idea: A rickety machine of meshing gears: each gear's teeth strike notes, so the gear ratios become polyrhythms, and the machine wobbles because nothing stays still.
how: Press PLAY. The motor (red) drives a chain of meshing gears. A gear with more teeth turns more slowly, so the ratios between gears create polyrhythms. Every tooth that passes the striker at the top of a gear plays that gear's sound (the big gears play your sample). Click a gear to change its number of teeth. ADD GEAR attaches another to the chain and CRANK sets the motor speed. WOBBLE makes the machine rickety, with loose teeth and slipping timing, because, as Tinguely said, nothing stays still.

manifesto.name: Für Statik (For Statics)
manifesto.author: Jean Tinguely
manifesto.where: leaflets thrown from an aeroplane over Düsseldorf in March 1959
ideas: Everything moves; stillness does not exist. Stop resisting change and be in time with the moment.
Art as moving, noisy machines (méta-mécaniques), often made of scrap.
Machines that break and even destroy themselves, as in Homage to New York at MoMA (1960).
quotes: Everything moves continuously. Immobility does not exist.
manifesto.system: There is no grid and no pattern, only rotating gears whose ratios produce rhythm. With WOBBLE on, the machine slips and rattles like one of Tinguely's scrap machines.

design.name: Armin Hofmann
design.who: Armin Hofmann, Swiss designer and teacher at the Basel School of Design
hallmarks: Black and white contrast with very few elements
Dot, line and form studies, with dynamic tension between shapes
Sans type (often Akzidenz or Univers) and a clear hierarchy
works: Graphic Design Manual: Principles and Practice (1965)
Giselle poster for the Basel Freilichtspiele (1959)
Posters for the Basel Stadttheater (1960s)

title: Décollage
idea: Three posters pasted on top of each other, each one a different groove; tear strips away to reveal the layers underneath.
how: Press PLAY. The wall has three posters pasted on top of each other. Each poster is a complete loop, from the top layer (a brass-band march) down to a jazz layer and finally your sample, pasted first on the bare wall. Only the parts you can see are heard: the horizontal axis is time in the loop and the vertical axis is the pitch range. Drag across the wall to tear the paper away and reveal what is underneath. PASTE glues a fresh top poster over everything. The torn shapes are the composition.

manifesto.name: Nouveau Réalisme manifestos
manifesto.author: Pierre Restany
manifesto.where: first manifesto published in Milan in April 1960; the group's declaration was signed at Yves Klein's flat in Paris on 27 October 1960
ideas: A 'new perceptual approach to the real': appropriating the real world of the city instead of painting it.
The sociological reality of the street: posters, scrap, packaging and consumer objects.
Raymond Hains and Jacques Villeglé's décollages: they presented posters torn off the walls of Paris as art.
manifesto.system: You do not write anything. The layers are found, readymade music, and you compose only by tearing, so what you hear is whatever the torn shape reveals.

design.name: Polish School of Posters
design.who: The Polish School of Posters: Henryk Tomaszewski, Jan Lenica, Roman Cieślewicz, Franciszek Starowieyski and others
hallmarks: Painterly, hand-drawn letters and shapes rather than photography
Surreal, witty metaphors and collage
Bold flat colour on rough paper, with torn edges
works: Henryk Tomaszewski's Henry Moore exhibition poster (1959)
Jan Lenica's Wozzeck poster for the Warsaw opera (1964)
Roman Cieślewicz's poster for Hitchcock's Vertigo (1963)

title: Poor Means
idea: Four poor materials (wire, stone, water and rag) and only the energy of your hands: pluck, strike, drip and rub.
how: Press PLAY. The table has four poor materials. WIRE: drag across the wires to pluck them (a physically modelled string, tuned by its length). STONE: click the stones to strike them. WATER: hold the mouse down on the bowl to let it drip. RAG: rub back and forth on the rag, and your sample is played at the speed and direction of your hand, like scratching. In the background, a slow ENERGY pulse runs through everything, like Giovanni Anselmo's twisted or tensioned works: the harder you play, the more energy builds up and the more the pulse rises.

manifesto.name: Arte Povera: Notes for a Guerrilla War
manifesto.author: Germano Celant
manifesto.where: Flash Art, Milan, November–December 1967; the same year as Celant's Arte Povera exhibition in Genoa
